source_quote: 3-Benzylidene Camphor is currently authorised for use in cosmetic products as a UV filter in a concentration up to maximum 2,0 %. It is listed under reference number 19 of Annex VI to Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009. ... Considering that 3-Benzylidene Camphor is known not only as a UV filter but also as a UV absorber, its use should be banned in cosmetic products. ... in Annex VI the entry concerning reference number 19 is deleted.
note: DIRECTIONAL A->B. A is in the library but is NO LONGER a permitted EU UV filter: Regulation (EU) 2015/1298 deleted Annex VI entry 19 and added A to Annex II (prohibited) as reference number 1379. So this is NOT a regulatory_class pair. The quoted recitals establish A was a regulated UV filter/UV absorber; B is a currently permitted Annex VI filter (entry 4). Both give photoprotection by the same mechanism - UV absorption by an organic chromophore - which is why B is a legal stand-in for A. No source I could fetch names a specific replacement for A, so this is mechanism-based, not a documented replacement. Weaker than the regulatory_class rows; treat accordingly.

source_quote: In Europe, low frequencies of sensitization have been observed to all releasers: 2-bromo-2-nitropropane-1,3-diol 0.4-1.2%, diazolidinyl urea 0.5-1.4%, imidazolidinyl urea 0.3-1.4%, quaternium-15 0.6-1.9% (for DMDM hydantoin no recent data are available).
note: I read only the abstract (retrieved via NCBI E-utilities efetch for PMID 20136875), not the full text. The quoted sentence groups 2-bromo-2-nitropropane-1,3-diol (= Bronopol, the Annex V glossary name for CAS 52-51-7) and DMDM hydantoin as members of the same class, 'the releasers'. Two further sources I fetched and read corroborate the class: (a) Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/1181, recital (2), verbatim: 'Certain of those preservatives are gradually releasing formaldehyde in order to fulfil a preserving function in the final cosmetic product (so called formaldehyde releasers).' (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX%3A32022R1181); (b) SCCS/1632/21 (https://health.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2022-08/sccs_o_254.pdf) p.7, quoting de Groot: 'all releasers (with the exception of 2-bromo-2-nitropropane-1,3-diol, for which adequate data are lacking) can, in the right circumstances of concentration and product composition, release >200 ppm formaldehyde...' and p.8 describing a study dosing 'DMDM hydantoin, releasing at least 40 ppm'. Caveat for the evaluation: bronopol's primary antimicrobial action is thiol oxidation; formaldehyde release is a shared secondary property, and the amount released by bronopol is explicitly described as not adequately characterised. This pair is also a regulatory_class pair (Annex V entries 21 and 33).

note: Strongest row in this class. The two esters are co-listed in ONE Annex III entry (376) with identical limits and an identical shared warning — verbatim from the same fetched Annex: "For any cosmetic product containing Retinol, Retinyl Acetate or Retinyl Palmitate the following, labelling is obligatory: 'Contains Vitamin A. Consider your daily intake before use'." CAVEAT the caller must not lose: the regulatory co-listing is on vitamin-A overexposure grounds, and recital (1) calls them "skin conditioning agents", NOT depigmenting agents. The anti-pigmentation relevance comes from a separate source I fetched — Pharmaceuticals 2025;18(3):368, doi:10.3390/ph18030368 (PMC11945762), verbatim: "Retinol was the most frequently used depigmenting agent (8.5%), followed by retinal, with a usage frequency of 2.8%." — plus that review's statement that "retinoids" are among the top-ten most-used depigmenting agents. AAPS PharmSciTech. 2014;15(2):354-63. doi:10.1208/s12249-013-0066-7 (PMID 24395400)
source_quote: a penetration retardation effect on percutaneous absorption of MTZ was observed for the formulations containing 1,2-diols having six- to seven-carbon chain in the presence of 1,4-cyclohexanediol (1,2-hexanediol with chain length of six hydrocarbons, RRs are 0.69 and 0.76 in the concentration of 4% and 1%, respectively; 1,2-heptanediol with chain length of seven hydrocarbons, RR is 0.78 in the concentration of 1%)
note: Both members are named explicitly in a source I retrieved and read. Two WebFetch passes over this paper gave contradicting answers about whether 1,2-heptanediol was studied, so I downloaded the PMC page and grepped the raw text myself — 16 hits, heptanediol is genuinely in the study. The paper places C6 and C7 together as a behaviourally matched sub-group (RR 0.69/0.76 vs 0.78) and separates them from the shorter homologues C3-C5, which showed no retardation; that is what makes hexanediol/heptanediol the defensible pair rather than any longer span of the series. HONEST LIMITS: source_type is set to 'review_article' only because the enum has no slot for a primary research article — this is an original study, not a review. It measures penetration modulation in hairless-mouse skin, not formulator substitution, and the authors synthesised 1,2-heptanediol in their own lab rather than sourcing it as a cosmetic raw material. So the row is a genuine same-mechanism/homologous-series claim, but it is weaker than the retinoid row and I did not find a source that states in so many words that a formulator swaps one for the other. Neither compound is covered by the CIR 1,2-glycols monograph used for the pair below (0 hits for heptanediol in that document).
